title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
statement: Given an unsorted integer array and an integer k, return the kth largest element. Can you do it without fully sorting the array?

nearMiss.why: The array is unsorted; sorting first is the O(n log n) baseline the follow-up asks you to beat.
Two heaps track the middle (median) of a stream; one size-k heap is enough for the kth largest.
Next-greater relationships don't rank elements globally.

trigger.why: 'kth largest' ⇒ size-k min-heap (O(n log k)) or quickselect (O(n) average).

ds.answer: PriorityQueue<Integer> min-heap capped at size k

wrong.t: PriorityQueue<Integer> max-heap of all n elements
wrong.why: Works, but O(n + k log n) with O(n) space; the size-k min-heap is the expected answer.

ds.why: The root of a size-k min-heap is the kth largest. TreeSet would also drop duplicates.

invariant.answer: The heap holds the k largest elements seen so far; its root is the smallest of them, i.e. the current kth largest.
wrong: The heap holds the k smallest elements seen so far.
The heap's root is the largest element seen.
The heap holds every element greater than the root's initial value.
invariant.why: Anything smaller than the root can't be in the top k.

time.why: n pushes and pops on a heap of size k. (Quickselect: O(n) average.)

wrong: Binary search can't find the largest element.
Binary search needs k to be a power of two.
Binary search only works on arrays without duplicates.

approach: Push each number into a min-heap; pop when size > k. Return the root. Alternative: quickselect with a random pivot.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
statement: Given an integer array and k, return the k most frequent elements in any order. Your solution must be better than O(n log n).

nearMiss.why: Counting needs a map, but a map alone doesn't select the top k; that step is the heap (or bucket sort).
Frequency is global over the array, not within a contiguous window.
Two heaps balance halves for a median; top-k needs one bounded heap.

trigger.why: 'k most …' ⇒ count, then keep a size-k heap ordered by count (or bucket by count).

ds.answer: HashMap<Integer, Integer> counts + PriorityQueue<int[]> min-heap by count, size k
ds.why: Count in O(n), select in O(u log k) for u distinct values. Bucket sort by count is the O(n) alternative.

invariant.answer: The heap holds the k highest-count elements seen so far; the root has the lowest count among them.
wrong: The heap holds the k elements with the largest values.
The heap root is the most frequent element.
The heap contains every distinct element.
invariant.why: Any element with a smaller count than the root is not in the top k.

time.why: Counting is O(n); heap work O(u log k) with u ≤ n.

wrong: Hash maps are O(n log n) per lookup.
A HashMap would return the k largest values instead.

approach: Count with a map. Push (value, count) into a min-heap by count; pop when size > k. Return the heap's values. Or bucket sort: buckets[count] lists, read from high counts.

title: Find Median from Data Stream
statement: Design a structure that supports addNum(num) for a stream of integers and findMedian() returning the median of all numbers added so far. Both should be efficient for many calls.

nearMiss.why: Binary-search insertion into a sorted list finds the slot in O(log n) but shifting elements makes each insert O(n).
One heap gives an extreme (min or max), not the middle.
Quickselect per query is O(n) each time; the stream needs incremental updates.

trigger.answer: median of all numbers added so far
trigger.why: Running median ⇒ max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half.

ds.answer: PriorityQueue<Integer> max-heap (low half) + PriorityQueue<Integer> min-heap (high half)
ds.why: Tops of the two heaps are the middle elements. TreeSet would also lose duplicates.

invariant.answer: max(low) ≤ min(high), and low has the same number of elements as high or one more.
wrong: Both heaps always hold the same number of elements.
low holds the newest half of the stream.
invariant.why: Then the median is low's top, or the average of both tops.

wrong: addNum O(1), findMedian O(n log n)
time.why: A constant number of heap operations per insert.

wrong: Binary search can't find a median.
Binary search needs the stream to be finite.
Binary search would need two arrays.

approach: Add to low; move low's top to high; if high is bigger, move its top back to low. Median = low.peek() (odd) or (low.peek() + high.peek()) / 2.0.

title: IPO
statement: You start with capital w and may finish at most k projects. Each project has a required capital and a profit that is added to your capital when done. Choose projects to maximise final capital.

nearMiss.why: Capital grows after each project, so this isn't a fixed-capacity knapsack; greedily taking the best affordable project is optimal.
Trying every order of k projects is exponential.
Projects have no start/end times to sort and merge.

trigger.answer: a profit that is added to your capital
trigger.why: Affordable set grows over time: keep unaffordable projects in a min-heap by capital, move them into a max-heap by profit as capital rises, take the best.

ds.answer: PriorityQueue<int[]> min-heap by capital + PriorityQueue<Integer> max-heap by profit
ds.why: One heap gates projects by requirement, the other picks the most profitable unlocked one.

invariant.answer: Every project with capital ≤ w is in the profit heap; every other project waits in the capital heap.
wrong: The profit heap holds all projects from the start.
Projects are taken in input order.
The capital heap holds completed projects.
invariant.why: Then taking the profit heap's top is always the best affordable choice.

time.why: Each project moves between heaps once; k pops.

wrong: Knapsack only works when capitals are sorted.

approach: Sort/heap projects by capital. Repeat k times: move every project with capital ≤ w into a max-heap by profit; if empty stop; w += pop.

title: Meeting Rooms III
statement: There are n rooms numbered 0..n−1. Meetings with unique start times are assigned in start order to the lowest-numbered free room; if none is free, the meeting is delayed until the earliest room frees up, keeping its duration. Return the room that held the most meetings.

nearMiss.why: The assignment rule is fixed (lowest free room), so there's nothing to choose; the difficulty is simulating it efficiently.
Rooms aren't merged into groups; they cycle between free and busy.
There's no contiguous window property; it's an event simulation.

wrong: the room that held the most meetings
trigger.why: Two orderings at once: free rooms by number, busy rooms by end time ⇒ two min-heaps.

ds.answer: PriorityQueue<Integer> free rooms by index + PriorityQueue<long[]> busy rooms by (endTime, index)
wrong: int[] next free time scanned linearly
ds.why: Scanning all n rooms per meeting is O(m · n); heaps make each step O(log n). Use long for end times.

invariant.answer: Before assigning a meeting, every room whose meeting ended by its start time has been moved from busy to free.
wrong: Free rooms are always kept in the order they became free.
Busy rooms are ordered by room number.
A delayed meeting keeps its original end time.
invariant.why: Then the free heap's top is the lowest-numbered available room; if empty, the busy heap's top frees first.

time.answer: O(m log m + m log n)
time.why: Sort meetings, then constant heap operations per meeting.

wrong: Greedy needs meetings sorted by end time.

approach: Sort by start. For each meeting: release busy rooms with end ≤ start into free. If free is non-empty, take its smallest room; else pop the earliest-ending busy room and shift the meeting to start at that end. Count per room.

title: Merge k Sorted Lists
statement: You are given k linked lists, each sorted in ascending order. Merge them into one sorted linked list and return it.

nearMiss.why: Two pointers merge TWO lists; merging k lists one by one is O(N · k).
Sorting all values again ignores that every list is already sorted: O(N log N).
The pointer work is easy; the hard part is picking the smallest head among k quickly.

trigger.why: k sorted sources and you always need the smallest current head ⇒ heap of heads.

ds.answer: PriorityQueue<ListNode> ordered by val, plus a dummy head
wrong: ArrayList<Integer> of all values then sort
ds.why: Comparator.comparingInt(n -> n.val); poll the smallest, offer its next.

invariant.answer: The heap holds exactly one unconsumed node from each non-empty list, so its root is the smallest remaining node overall.
wrong: The heap holds all N nodes at once.
The heap is ordered by list index.
The heap's root is the largest remaining node.
invariant.why: Each list's next element can only be ≥ its current head.

time.answer: O(N log k), N = total nodes
time.why: N polls and offers on a heap of size k.

space.why: The heap (the output reuses the input nodes).

wrong: Two pointers can't work on linked lists.
Two pointers only work on arrays of equal length.
Two pointers would lose the sorted order.

approach: Offer all non-null heads to a min-heap. Poll the smallest, append to tail, offer its next. Return dummy.next. (Divide-and-conquer pairwise merging is also O(N log k).)

twists.statement: Given the heads of two sorted linked lists, splice them into one sorted list and return its head.

nearMiss.why: With two lists the heap only ever compares two heads: comparing them directly is simpler and O(1) space.
Nothing is ranked; the order already exists in the inputs.
Nothing is split around a pivot.

twists.why: Two sorted lists ⇒ dummy head and pick the smaller head each step.
twists.approach: dummy, tail; while both: tail.next = smaller; advance. Attach the rest.

title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
statement: Given two integer arrays sorted in ascending order and an integer k, return the k pairs (u, v), with u from the first array and v from the second, that have the smallest sums.

nearMiss.why: Two pointers can't enumerate pairs in sum order: the next-smallest pair may move either index.
Generating all m · n pairs and sorting is O(mn log mn).
Binary searching a sum threshold can count pairs, but listing exactly k in order is simpler with a heap.

trigger.why: Each u defines a sorted list of pairs (u, v₀), (u, v₁), …; you want the k smallest across those lists ⇒ k-way merge.

ds.answer: PriorityQueue<int[]> of {sum, i, j} seeded with (i, 0) for the first k values of i
ds.why: When (i, j) is popped, push (i, j + 1): the next element of that row's list.

invariant.answer: The heap holds the next unseen pair from each row list; the root is the smallest unseen pair overall.
wrong: The heap holds all m · n pairs.
The heap is ordered by i.
Pairs are popped in order of v.
invariant.why: Within a row, sums only increase as j increases.

time.why: At most k pops and k pushes on a heap of size ≤ k.

wrong: Two pointers would return pairs from the same array.

approach: Push (nums1[i] + nums2[0], i, 0) for i < min(k, m). Repeat k times: pop (s, i, j), record the pair, push (i, j + 1) if j + 1 < n.

title: K Closest Points to Origin
statement: Given a list of points on a plane and an integer k, return the k points closest to the origin (Euclidean distance), in any order.

nearMiss.why: There are no sorted lists to merge; it's selection of the k smallest from one unsorted list.
Binary-searching a distance threshold works but is fiddly; a size-k heap or quickselect is direct.
Points aren't ranges; nothing overlaps.

trigger.answer: the k points closest to the origin
trigger.why: k smallest by a key ⇒ size-k max-heap (or quickselect, average O(n)).

ds.answer: PriorityQueue<int[]> max-heap by x² + y², capped at size k
wrong: Min-heap of all n points, then poll k
ds.why: Compare squared distances: no sqrt, no doubles. A min-heap of all n is O(n + k log n): fine, but the capped max-heap is O(k) space.

invariant.answer: The heap holds the k closest points seen so far, and its top is the farthest of them; a closer point replaces it.
wrong: The heap is sorted by x-coordinate.
The heap top is the closest point seen so far.
The heap holds every point at distance < k.
invariant.why: Max-heap of size k = the top is the eviction candidate.

time.why: Each point does an O(log k) offer/poll. Quickselect is O(n) average.

wrong: k-way merge would return the k farthest points.

approach: Max-heap by squared distance; offer each point; if size > k poll. Return the heap contents.

title: Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers
statement: Worker i has quality q[i] and minimum wage w[i]. Hire exactly k workers: each must be paid at least their minimum wage, and pay within the group must be proportional to quality. Return the least total cost.

nearMiss.why: Sorting by wage/quality ratio is the greedy half, but you still need the k smallest qualities among workers with ratio ≤ the current one: that's a heap.
Only one heap is needed (largest quality to evict); there's no median or two-sided balance.
It looks like choosing a subset, but the cost structure (ratio × total quality) makes a sort + heap exact; no DP table.

trigger.answer: pay within the group must be proportional to quality
trigger.why: Proportional pay ⇒ the group's rate is set by its max wage/quality ratio; cost = ratio × sum of qualities. Sweep ratios ascending, keep the k smallest qualities in a max-heap.

ds.answer: Workers sorted by w/q, plus PriorityQueue<Integer> max-heap of qualities (Comparator.reverseOrder()) and a running quality sum
wrong: Min-heap of wages of size k
ds.why: Evict the largest quality when the heap exceeds k.

invariant.answer: When processing worker i (sorted by ratio), the heap holds the k smallest qualities among workers 0..i, so cost = ratio_i × qualitySum is the best group with captain i.
wrong: The heap holds the k cheapest minimum wages.
The ratio decreases as i increases.
Every worker in the heap is paid exactly their minimum wage.
invariant.why: Worker i's ratio is the max in the group, so everyone is paid at least their minimum.

wrong: Greedy would hire the k cheapest workers, which is optimal.

approach: Sort workers by w/q. For each: push q, sum += q; if size > k sum −= poll(); if size == k best = min(best, sum × ratio).

title: Last Stone Weight
statement: Repeatedly take the two heaviest stones and smash them: equal stones both vanish, otherwise the lighter vanishes and the heavier loses that much weight. Return the weight of the last stone, or 0 if none remain.

nearMiss.why: That's Last Stone Weight II, where you choose pairings. Here the rule is fixed: always the two heaviest.
The rule is already given; the question is how to fetch the two heaviest repeatedly in O(log n).
Sorting once doesn't help: the remainder must be re-inserted in order every round.

wrong: the weight of the last stone
trigger.why: Repeatedly extract the max and re-insert a new value ⇒ max-heap.

ds.why: TreeSet would lose equal weights; a heap keeps duplicates.

invariant.answer: The heap always holds exactly the stones still alive, with the heaviest on top.
wrong: The heap size halves every round.
The heap top is always the original heaviest stone.
The heap holds stones in insertion order.
invariant.why: Each round removes two and may add one.

time.why: At most n rounds of O(log n).

wrong: Knapsack would give the heaviest last stone.

approach: Heap all stones. While size > 1: a = poll, b = poll; if a != b offer a − b. Return isEmpty ? 0 : peek.

twists.change: You choose which two stones to smash each time.
twists.statement: Stones have weights. Each turn you choose any two stones and smash them (the difference survives, or nothing if equal). Return the smallest possible weight of the final stone.
twists.ds: boolean[] (or BitSet) of reachable subset sums up to total / 2

nearMiss.why: Always smashing the two heaviest is one fixed strategy, not the best one.
No local rule is optimal; the result is a split into two groups with a minimal difference.
Trying every smashing order is exponential; subset sums capture all outcomes.

twists.why: Any smashing order ends as (sum of one group) − (sum of the other) ⇒ find the subset sum closest to total / 2.
twists.approach: dp[0] = true; for w: for s from total/2 down to w: dp[s] |= dp[s − w]. Answer = total − 2 · (largest reachable s).

title: Sliding Window Median
statement: Given an integer array and a window size k, return the median of every contiguous window of size k as the window slides from left to right.

nearMiss.why: A monotonic deque gives the window max or min, not the middle element.
The window part is easy; the hard part is a running median, which needs two balanced halves.
One heap gives only one end; a median needs the boundary between the lower and upper halves.

trigger.answer: the median of every contiguous window
trigger.why: Running median ⇒ two heaps; sliding ⇒ removals too (lazy deletion, or TreeMap/TreeSet halves in Java).

ds.answer: Two halves: max-heap low, min-heap high (with lazy-delete counts) or two TreeSet<Integer> of indices ordered by value
ds.why: PriorityQueue.remove(Object) is O(k); a TreeSet ordered by (value, index) removes in O(log k).

invariant.answer: Every value in low ≤ every value in high, and low has the same size as high or one more; the median comes from their tops.
wrong: low holds the first half of the window by position.
Both heaps are always the same size.
high's top is always the newest element.
invariant.why: Add, remove the outgoing element, then rebalance.

wrong: O(n log n) regardless of k
time.why: Each slide does O(1) heap/set operations of O(log k).

space.why: The two halves (plus pending lazy deletions).

wrong: A monotonic deque would give the median of the whole array.
Monotonic deques only work for k = 2.

approach: Keep low (max side) and high (min side) as TreeSets of indices compared by (value, index). Insert the new index, remove i − k, rebalance sizes, read the median from low.last() / high.first() (use long or double to avoid overflow).

title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
statement: In an n × n matrix every row and every column is sorted ascending. Return the k-th smallest element overall, using less than O(n²) memory.

nearMiss.why: A size-k heap over all n² cells ignores the sorted rows and reads everything; seeding one pointer per row is the k-way merge.
Rows aren't chained end to end, so you can't search the matrix as one flat sorted array.
No in-place traversal trick; the order comes from merging sorted rows.

trigger.answer: every row and every column is sorted
trigger.why: n sorted lists + k-th smallest ⇒ k-way merge with a min-heap of row heads (or binary search on the value with a staircase count).

ds.answer: PriorityQueue<int[]> of {value, row, col} ordered by value, seeded with column 0 of each row
wrong: Max-heap of size k over all cells
ds.why: Poll k − 1 times, pushing the next cell in the same row.

invariant.answer: The heap holds the smallest unconsumed cell of each row; after i polls, the i smallest elements have been removed in order.
wrong: The heap holds the k largest values.
Each poll removes a whole row.
The heap top is always on the diagonal.
invariant.why: Same invariant as merging k sorted lists.

time.why: k polls on a heap of at most n entries.

wrong: A heap can't hold matrix cells.
Heaps need the matrix to be square.
A top-k heap would return the k-th largest instead.

approach: Offer (matrix[r][0], r, 0) for each row. Poll k − 1 times, offering (matrix[r][c+1], r, c+1) when c + 1 < n. Return the top value.

title: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists
statement: You have k lists of integers, each sorted ascending. Find the smallest range [a, b] that includes at least one number from each of the k lists (ties broken by the smaller a).

nearMiss.why: With two lists, two pointers suffice; with k lists you need the minimum of k heads at every step, which is a heap.
The answer is a range, but the inputs are points in sorted lists, not intervals to merge.
We're not selecting k largest; the heap holds one current element per list while advancing the minimum.

trigger.answer: at least one number from each of the k lists
wrong: ties broken by the smaller a
trigger.why: One pointer per sorted list + always advance the smallest ⇒ k-way merge, tracking the current max alongside the heap's min.

ds.answer: PriorityQueue<int[]> of {value, list, index} ordered by value, plus an int currentMax
wrong: TreeMap<Integer, Integer> value → list over all values
int[] merged array with HashMap counts only
ds.why: Merging everything then sliding a window with counts also works (the alternate).

invariant.answer: The heap holds exactly one element from every list, so [heap min, currentMax] always covers all k lists; advancing the min is the only way to shrink it.
wrong: The heap holds the k smallest values overall.
Each list is fully consumed before the next.
invariant.why: Stop when the list of the polled minimum is exhausted.

time.answer: O(N log k), N = total elements
time.why: Each element enters the heap once.

wrong: Two pointers can't handle negative numbers.
Two pointers need the lists merged first, which is impossible.
Two pointers would find the largest range.

approach: Seed the heap with each list's first element, max = largest of them. Loop: poll min; update best if max − min is smaller; if its list has a next element, offer it and update max; else stop.
